strengths: Originality: Dynamically forking and pruning intermediate residual streams is an interesting architectural contribution. Coupling routing scores to attention, residual updates, and output mixing offers a plausible way to learn allocation using only language-modeling loss.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers two pretraining corpora and three model sizes. Table 1 reports consistent perplexity improvements for the larger routing budget; at 772M on OpenWebText, perplexity improves from 21.22 to 19.74 and LAMBADA accuracy from 23.9 to 29.4.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architectural diagrams, routing equations, and appendix tables provide useful implementation detail, including model dimensions, optimization settings, tokenizer, and training hardware.

Limitations and ethics: The paper openly acknowledges wall-clock inefficiency, routing-gradient difficulties, and limited reasoning evaluation. These acknowledgments are appropriate, and the manuscript presents no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—causal validity is unresolved. Section 2.3 selects the top routing scores across the entire sequence. Consequently, changing future tokens can change whether an earlier token retains or creates a fork, affecting its prediction despite causal attention masking. Section 2.6 scores complete sequences this way, so the principal perplexity and likelihood-based evaluations are not established as valid autoregressive comparisons. Scaling the budget with sequence length does not eliminate this dependency. Figure 6 provides encouraging prefix-based evidence for one model on a smaller subset, but does not validate the main results across settings. A suffix-invariance test and comprehensive prefix-only evaluation are needed.

Soundness—experiments do not isolate adaptive allocation. Thoughtbubbles changes routing, attention/value attenuation, residual gating, positional encoding, and output probability mixing simultaneously. The copy baselines decode only the rightmost residual, whereas the proposed model mixes predictions from multiple streams. Without uniform/random routing and matched gating/output-mixing controls, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to learned allocation.

Significance—reasoning and inference-time scaling claims exceed the evidence. The experiments primarily establish language-modeling improvements; they do not demonstrate that increasing inference compute for a fixed trained model improves difficult reasoning. Figure 6 tests budget handling across prefix lengths, rather than a reasoning quality–compute curve. Entropy correlations and attention magnitudes are suggestive but do not establish that forks perform useful reasoning or exclude simple allocation heuristics.

Compute comparisons are insufficiently quantified. Copy-5 is described as roughly FLOPs-matched, but actual training/inference FLOPs, memory, throughput, and latency are not reported. The extra vocabulary projections used for output mixing also matter. A compute-matched standard-transformer training baseline would help determine whether the additional computation is well spent. The acknowledged implementation inefficiency is not itself disqualifying, but practical efficiency remains unestablished.

Presentation contains substantive contradictions. Appendix B reports lower perplexity with extended forking (28.02 versus 29.84), while its caption describes extended forking as worse and Section 8 invokes this ablation to support a gradient-bottleneck explanation. The stated layer schedules also conflict. Table 1 duplicates the 150M OpenWebText κ=2L label, and the claim of outperforming baselines on all LAMBADA/HellaSwag evaluations has counterexamples, including 150M peS2o with κ=2L.

Reproducibility and uncertainty remain incomplete. No seeds, repeated-run variability, or confidence intervals are reported, although several downstream differences are small. Dataset versions and exact validation splits, routing-function architecture, and the handling of top-k when fewer than κ candidates exist need specification. The manuscript states that a PyTorch implementation is released but supplies no identifiable project repository. These omissions compound the unresolved evaluation issue and prevent a technically solid acceptance recommendation.

strengths: Originality: Dynamically forking and pruning residual streams between transformer blocks is an interesting architectural contribution. Combining cumulative routing scores, score-dependent attenuation, and output mixing provides a plausible way to learn parallel computation using only language-modeling loss.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates three model sizes, two pretraining corpora, and both standard-transformer and duplicated-token baselines. Table 1 reports consistent perplexity improvements for the larger forking budget, with substantial LAMBADA gains in several settings.

Soundness: The prefix-based autoregressive experiment in Figure 6 is valuable supporting evidence: dynamic-budget inference achieves perplexity 21.18 versus 22.15 for the baseline on the evaluated subset. This suggests some benefit survives beyond blockwise evaluation.

Presentation and transparency: The architectural diagrams and equations explain the main mechanism, and Appendix A supplies useful training configurations. The limitations openly acknowledge wall-clock inefficiency, routing-gradient difficulties, and the absence of strong reasoning evaluations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—global routing compromises causal evaluation: Equations 4–6 select surviving streams through top-k competition across the entire input sequence. Consequently, future tokens can change which streams survive at earlier positions, even if attention itself is causally masked. Section 2.6 scores complete sequences, so the main blockwise perplexities are not established as valid autoregressive likelihoods comparable to the baseline. Scaling the budget proportionally to sequence length does not remove this dependence. Figure 6 partially addresses the concern, but only for one configuration on an unspecified smaller subset. The principal results require prefix-only reevaluation or a demonstrably causal routing mechanism.

Soundness—adaptivity is not isolated: Thoughtbubbles differs from the copy baselines in routing, intermediate insertion, attenuation, positional treatment, and probability averaging; the copy baseline decodes only the rightmost stream. Without fixed or random routing controls using the same remaining components, and an output-averaging ablation, the experiments cannot attribute improvements specifically to learned adaptive allocation. Attention to sibling streams and entropy correlations are suggestive, but do not establish that routing identifies computational difficulty or that additional forks causally improve predictions.

Significance—compute and reasoning claims exceed the evidence: The comparisons are described as roughly FLOPs-matched without quantitative accounting for routing, expanded attention, and per-stream vocabulary decoding. There are no measured throughput, latency, memory, or equal-time comparisons. Separately trained models with different budgets do not establish inference-time scaling for a fixed checkpoint. The general language-modeling results support a potentially useful specialized contribution, but not the conclusion that the method solves harder tasks through scalable reasoning computation.

Presentation—material contradictions undermine interpretation: Table 4 reports better perplexity with extended forking, 28.02 versus 29.84, while its caption says extended forking is worse and the limitations invoke this ablation to motivate a gradient-bottleneck explanation. The stated layer schedules are also inconsistent. Table 1 repeats the 2L label for both 150M OpenWebText variants. Claims of superiority on all LAMBADA and HellaSwag evaluations and over parameter-matched BLiMP baselines also have counterexamples in Table 1.

Reproducibility: Although the manuscript says a PyTorch implementation is released, it provides no identifiable link to that implementation. Important details remain unclear, including the parameterization of the routing function, handling top-k when fewer than κ candidates exist, and precise validation splits and autoregressive-subset construction. The CLUTRR qualitative example lacks a corresponding experimental protocol.

Statistical support: Results lack repeated-run variability or uncertainty estimates. Several HellaSwag and PIQA differences are small, and performance sometimes declines, so the broad downstream-improvement claims are insufficiently supported. Together with the causal-routing issue, these weaknesses prevent the reported evidence from reliably establishing the central claims in the current submission.

strengths: Originality: Learning to insert and prune intermediate residual streams using only language-modeling loss is an interesting architectural contribution. Coupling routing scores to attention, residual updates, and output mixing provides a concrete mechanism for learning adaptive parallel computation.

Significance: The reported experiments cover two pretraining corpora and three model sizes. At 772M parameters on OpenWebText, the larger-budget model improves perplexity from 21.22 to 19.74 and LAMBADA accuracy from 23.9 to 29.4. Comparisons with duplicated-token baselines help establish that simply adding streams does not reproduce the reported gains.

Soundness: Section 5.1 usefully checks actual autoregressive evaluation rather than relying exclusively on blockwise scoring. Dynamic-budget autoregression achieves 21.18 perplexity versus 22.15 for the baseline on the evaluated subset, providing preliminary evidence that some benefit survives deployment.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main architectural pipeline is understandable, and Appendix A provides model dimensions, optimizer settings, tokenization, training budget, and hardware. The limitations discussion candidly acknowledges runtime overhead, routing-gradient difficulties, and the absence of substantial reasoning-task evaluation. There are no apparent material ethical concerns in the described research.
weaknesses: Soundness—causality is the decisive unresolved issue. Section 2.3 selects streams using top-k scores across the entire sequence. Consequently, changing a future token can change which earlier streams survive, their subsequent computation, and earlier output probabilities even with causal attention. Section 2.6 explicitly scores complete sequences this way. The resulting blockwise scores are therefore not guaranteed to be causal language-model probabilities, compromising their interpretation as perplexity and their comparison with causal baselines. Scaling the budget with sequence length does not eliminate this future-dependent competition. The encouraging autoregressive subset experiment does not validate the full evaluation suite; the paper needs a causal routing formulation or comprehensive prefix-only evaluation and a suffix-invariance check.

Soundness—adaptive allocation is not isolated experimentally. The duplicated-token baseline decodes only the rightmost stream, whereas Thoughtbubbles mixes predictions from all surviving streams and also changes gating, positional encoding, and intermediate stream initialization. No controlled ablations separate these effects from learned allocation. Uniform or random intermediate routing with the same attenuation and output mixture would be particularly informative. Attention magnitudes and entropy correlations alone do not establish that routing selects locations where extra computation improves predictions.

Significance—the claims about difficult reasoning and inference-time scaling exceed the evidence. The experiments primarily establish language-modeling and modest zero-shot gains; they do not show improved multi-step reasoning or performance scaling when additional inference compute is supplied to one fixed trained model. The two training budgets do not establish test-time scaling, and Figure 6 actually shows degradation under a naively increased relative budget. The acknowledged resource limitations are reasonable, but the conclusions should be narrowed accordingly.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Compute matching is described as approximate without numerical FLOP accounting, throughput, or memory measurements. No equal-compute standard-transformer training comparison establishes the best use of the additional budget. There are also no reported repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates, which matters for small downstream differences. Despite announcing a PyTorch release, the manuscript provides no identifiable implementation link; dataset split construction and evaluation sample counts are insufficiently specified.

Presentation and evidential consistency: Appendix B reports lower perplexity with extended forking, 28.02 versus 29.84, yet its caption says extended forking is worse and Section 8 uses this experiment to motivate a gradient-bottleneck explanation. The stated layer schedules are also inconsistent. Table 1 labels both OpenWebText 150M configurations as κ = 2L, and the claim of improvement on all LAMBADA and HellaSwag evaluations has counterexamples, including 150M peS2o at κ = 2L. These discrepancies need correction before the empirical conclusions can be relied upon.

strengths: Originality: Learning to create and delete intermediate residual streams using only language-modeling loss is an interesting architectural contribution. The combination of cumulative routing scores, score-attenuated computation, and fork-aware positional embeddings offers a useful alternative to inserting a fixed number of pause tokens.

Significance: The reported language-modeling gains span two datasets and models from 150M to 1.9B parameters. In Table 1, the 20B-token model achieves perplexity 12.68 versus 15.03 for the 40B-token baseline, motivating further investigation of the approach.

Experimental breadth: The paper includes parameter-matched and duplicated-token baselines, component ablations, allocation visualizations, and an autoregressive evaluation. Figure 6 is particularly valuable because it demonstrates that some perplexity improvement persists under prefix-based evaluation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architectural overview and explicit routing equations make the main mechanism understandable. Appendices provide model configurations, optimization settings, positional encoding details, and benchmark scoring procedures.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion acknowledges inference-budget distribution shift and reduced allocation at the highest-entropy tokens. These are useful observations. No specific material research-ethics concern is apparent for this architectural study.
weaknesses: Soundness—causality is not preserved by the described blockwise routing. Section 2.3 selects streams using top-k scores across the entire sequence. Consequently, whether an earlier token retains a fork can depend on future tokens, even with causal attention. Section 2.6 explicitly scores complete sequences in one pass, so the resulting scores need not represent causal next-token probabilities. Scaling the budget proportionally to sequence length does not eliminate this dependency. Figure 6 provides encouraging prefix-based results on a small subset at one scale, but does not validate the main blockwise perplexities or sequence-scoring benchmarks. A suffix-invariance test and causal evaluation across the principal settings are necessary.

Soundness—the experiments do not isolate the benefit of learned adaptive allocation. Copy-3/Copy-5 differ from Thoughtbubbles in insertion depth, score attenuation, positional treatment, and output aggregation. The appendices ablate aggregation and attention attenuation, but do not compare learned routing against uniform or random routing with otherwise identical architecture and compute. Thus, gains cannot confidently be attributed to allocating computation to difficult tokens. Attention weights and entropy correlations also do not establish that those allocations causally improve reasoning.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence. Half the training tokens is not half the training compute or time when most layers process expanded sequences. Table 5 reports 327 ms versus 234 ms per training step, approximately 40% overhead, rather than nearly identical cost. This supports a possible efficiency advantage at half the token count, but not the abstract's unqualified half-budget claim. There is no comprehensive matched-FLOP comparison, end-to-end training timing on the actual TPU setup, or generation latency and memory evaluation. Global rerouting can also change earlier representations as the prefix grows, leaving KV-cache compatibility unresolved.

Presentation and empirical claims are inconsistent with the tables. The claim of outperforming every metric at half the token budget is contradicted by ARC-Challenge in Table 1: 24.50 versus 26.17. Table 2 also contains regressions, including LAMBADA and HellaSwag for the 150M peS2o model with κ = 2L, and several BLiMP and PIQA settings. GSM8K at half the pretraining budget is essentially tied, 31.50 versus 31.46; without uncertainty estimates, this is not convincing evidence of improvement. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported.

Significance—the demonstrated contribution is narrower than the inference-time reasoning claims. Comparing separately trained models with different budgets does not establish that a fixed model benefits from additional test-time computation. The fixed-budget inference experiment actually degrades perplexity, while dynamic budget scaling primarily restores the training ratio. A controlled inference-budget sweep and stronger reasoning evaluations are needed to substantiate the claimed ability to solve harder tasks through inference-time scaling.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in consequential places. GSM8K decoding settings, answer extraction, and the precise GSM8K-aug source and overlap controls are insufficiently specified. The additional 2B-token mid-training stage also needs clearer separation from the headline token budgets and checkpoint evaluations. Training settings conflict: Section 3.2 specifies 10% warmup, whereas Table 3 gives 1%, and the 1.9B batch configuration in Table 4 does not straightforwardly match Table 3. These gaps compound the causal-evaluation concern and prevent a reliable acceptance recommendation.

strengths: Originality: Learning to fork and prune intermediate residual streams using only language-modeling loss is an interesting architectural contribution. Cumulative scoring, score-dependent attenuation, and fractional positional encoding form a concrete approach to allocating parallel latent computation.

Significance: The reported perplexity improvements span two corpora and multiple model sizes. At 1.9B parameters, Table 1 reports substantial improvements in perplexity and HellaSwag, making the approach worth investigating even without the broader reasoning claims.

Soundness: The paper includes useful component ablations and an explicit comparison between blockwise and autoregressive evaluation. Figure 6 reports that dynamic-budget autoregression retains an advantage over the baseline on the tested subset, providing some evidence beyond blockwise scoring.

Presentation and reproducibility: The main mechanism is explained through equations and diagrams, and Appendix A supplies substantial architecture and optimization details. The discussion of short-prefix distribution shift and difficulties with deeper forking is helpful.
weaknesses: Soundness—causal validity is unresolved. Section 2.3 selects streams using top-k scores across the entire sequence. Consequently, changing future tokens can change which earlier streams survive, their positional encodings, and earlier predictions, despite causal attention masking. Section 2.6 explicitly scores complete sequences in one pass. Scaling the budget proportionally to sequence length does not remove this dependence. Figure 6's prefix-based experiment on one smaller-model subset is encouraging, but does not establish that the main perplexity and sequence-scoring results measure valid autoregressive likelihoods. A suffix-invariance test, a causally valid routing rule, and comprehensive prefix-only evaluation are needed.

Soundness—headline claims exceed the reported results. The assertion that the 20B-token model beats the 40B-token baseline on every metric contradicts Table 1: ARC-Challenge is 24.50 versus 26.17. Table 2 also contains regressions on BLiMP and PIQA, and some LAMBADA/HellaSwag settings. GSM8K at half the pretraining tokens is essentially tied, 31.50 versus 31.46; without uncertainty estimates, this supports competitive performance rather than a demonstrated improvement.

Efficiency is insufficiently established. Half as many training tokens does not mean half the training compute or time when intermediate sequence lengths increase. Table 5 reports 327 ms versus 234 ms per forward/backward pass, approximately 40% overhead. This suggests a possible overall saving at half the tokens, but does not substantiate the claimed halving of pretraining time. The paper lacks end-to-end training measurements on the actual TPU setup, detailed FLOP accounting, and generation latency or KV-cache analysis; rerouting earlier streams as prefixes grow makes the latter particularly relevant.

Originality and mechanism attribution: Copy-3/Copy-5 are useful controls, but differ from Thoughtbubbles in insertion depth, output aggregation, and attenuation as well as adaptivity. The ablations do not isolate learned allocation against uniform or random allocation with the same layerwise budget and otherwise identical architecture. Thus, the experiments do not establish how much benefit comes specifically from adaptive routing rather than extra streams or the changed output head.

Significance—the reasoning and inference-time scaling claims remain preliminary. The paper does not demonstrate a quality-versus-inference-budget curve for a fixed trained model. GSM8K follows substantial supervised mathematical mid-training and shows little improvement, while entropy correlations and qualitative fork visualizations do not establish that additional computation resolves difficult reasoning steps. These observations support learned allocation behavior, but not the stronger conclusion that the method solves tasks requiring scalable inference-time computation.

Reproducibility and presentation need improvement. There are no reported training-seed variations or confidence intervals, and Figure 6's subset size is unspecified. The GSM8K evaluation lacks sufficiently detailed prompting, decoding, and answer-extraction settings, and the provenance and train/test separation of GSM8K-aug need clarification. Configuration inconsistencies include the 10% warmup in Section 3.2 versus 1% in Table 3 and global batch size 480 versus 14 × 32 in Table 4. These issues make precise replication difficult. There is no evident material ethical violation, but clearer data provenance and benchmark-contamination safeguards are warranted.

strengths: Originality: Learned insertion and deletion of intermediate residual streams is an interesting architectural contribution. Combining cumulative scores, score-dependent attenuation, and output merging provides a concrete mechanism for learning adaptive allocation using language-modeling loss alone.

Significance: The reported results warrant further investigation. At 1.9B parameters, the 20B-token model achieves perplexity 12.68 versus 15.03 for the 40B-token baseline, and improves HellaSwag from 47.29 to 50.04 (Table 1). Experiments across multiple sizes and two additional pretraining corpora provide useful breadth.

Presentation and analysis: The architectural diagrams make the main idea accessible. Appendices provide model configurations, optimization details, component ablations, and timing measurements. The discussion openly acknowledges autoregressive distribution shift and reduced allocation at the highest entropy levels.
Research ethics: The work uses established datasets for a general architectural contribution, and no specific material ethical concern is apparent from the manuscript.
weaknesses: Soundness—causality is the decisive unresolved issue. Section 2.3 selects streams using top-k scores across the entire sequence. Consequently, changing future tokens can change which earlier streams survive, their positional encodings, and earlier predictions, even with causal attention. Section 2.6 explicitly scores complete sequences in one forward pass. Proportional budget scaling does not remove this dependency. Figure 6 provides encouraging prefix-based results on one small subset, but does not establish causal validity for the main training and evaluation pipeline. The paper needs a precise causal allocation rule, a suffix-invariance check, and prefix-only evaluation of the principal results.

Soundness—several headline claims contradict the tables. At half the pretraining tokens, ARC-Challenge is worse than baseline: 24.50 versus 26.17 (Table 1), despite repeated claims of improvement on every metric. GSM8K is effectively tied at 31.50 versus 31.46, with no uncertainty estimates. Table 2 also contains regressions on BLiMP, PIQA, and some LAMBADA/HellaSwag settings. These results support a narrower claim than universal superiority.

Soundness—adaptive allocation is insufficiently isolated. The copy baselines differ in placement, positional treatment, and output aggregation, while the smaller proposed models also use a mixture of output distributions. Appendix C establishes that attenuation and merging matter, but does not establish that learned allocation outperforms random or uniform intermediate forking under otherwise identical settings. Entropy correlations and attention magnitudes do not demonstrate that allocation identifies computational difficulty or causes the improvements.

Significance and efficiency—the evidence does not yet establish the advertised inference-time scaling benefit. There is no quality-versus-inference-budget curve for a fixed trained model. Half the training tokens also does not mean half the training time: Table 5 reports 327 ms versus 234 ms per forward/backward pass, approximately 40% overhead. This measurement suggests potentially useful training savings, but total training costs, matched-compute comparisons, and autoregressive latency are needed. Sequence-wide reallocation also leaves KV-cache compatibility unresolved.

Reproducibility: The claimed PyTorch and JAX release footnotes are blank in the supplied manuscript. GSM8K prompting, decoding, answer extraction, and the exact GSM8K-aug source and contamination controls are insufficiently specified. Training details contain inconsistencies, including 10% warmup in Section 3.2 versus 1% in Table 3. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, limiting interpretation of small downstream differences.

Presentation and limitations: The paper distinguishes blockwise and autoregressive behavior but does not confront the underlying future-dependent routing issue. Claims about overcoming bounded computation and solving harder tasks through inference-time scaling exceed the demonstrated evidence. The promising architectural idea and reported gains are therefore insufficient for acceptance without resolving the central validity concern.
